comments.author: @higgledypiggledycubledy8899
comments.text: When I was a child in the late eighties, having learned that a friend's mom had a computer at home for work, we decided to it was a great opportunity to create our own video game. So we drew a couple of levels on paper with some notes, and confidently asked the mother if she could please use her computer to "make it real". She had to explain to us it didn't work that way, then I learned about programming and always felt a little embarrassed having been so naive. I feel somehow vindicated, about 35 years later, that I wasn't foolish to imagine a computer should be able to do that, it's just that they weren't quite there yet. And it blows my mind to think that in a couple of years my son might make a similar request and I could say yeah sure, we have 10 minutes, let's make your game.

comments.author: @pmiddlet72
comments.text:
So something to keep in mind here. The low barrier to entry for arxiv papers is truly astounding. There are journal referees, but the extraordinary speed to which these papers are coming out defies explanation, and in my mind naturally sets off my usual bit of skeptical inquiry (which is important, at least in healthy doses).  The amount of time one's academic research finally goes into publication, at whatever step of the process that research is in far exceeds that of these papers. So we're left to the tech companies to give the greenlight on what papers  will ever see the light of public day (some of these articles simply read like white papers quite truthfully). 

The materials science hype may be real. But it is FAR to early to tell what compounds, alloys, etc. that GNoME has come up with will bear any fruit for any of the 'potential' claims  at all. These are at best hypothetical at this time. Materials development and testing are naturally the next steps. While there may be a de novo idea for a compound,  or even 1,000 compounds - they must still be developed and tested for their indicated use. Most things like this are usually fails in one form or another. Down the road, however, given the right feedback (and robust at that) I think we can reasonably conceive in the next few years that AIs like this will be able to learn from past failures and produce more 'hits'. 

Naturally, this is a problem of high dimension, much like the area of disease that Wes touched on. One can't just 'feed' in DNA and  the AI spit out cures for disease on a whim. This too is a highly multivariate and somewhat chaotic (as in nonlinearly dynamic)  problem. The DNA is just a reference text - no more, no less. A single set of chromosomes can never tell a person's story, without that person's history, the history of their descendants and ancestors, the history of neighbors, friends, related ethnic backgrounds, gender, socioeconomic status, geography, biological development from childhood to adult (that neither genetics nor epigenetics can explain - though clues they may give ).  

These types of problems I think can eventually be solved by AI/AGI,. In fact I think it's inevitable. But not right now - maybe in 3-5 years we'll have credible output (which is still blazing fast). But this won't happen when we are barely learning ourselves how to 'feed the machine' rigorously vetted information,. Even AI doesn't yet quite understand various forms of scientific bias and error, which is a slightly different animal from predicting the next word I'm going to say.  My gut tells me that if AI could get us fundamentally to 30% reproducible research in the next  5-7 yrs vs the current roughly 10% - THAT will be an enormous leap worthy of applause - though lay investors and the layfolk-at-large may not truly grasp the magnitude of that.

I predicted this over a decade ago back when I was a teenager, but I didn't think they would be making new crystals as such. I thought it would be new enzymes.
In hindsight enzymes are a much harder problem than new crystals;
Crystals just requires an 'understanding'(? not sure if thats the right word) of atomic interactions but enzymes need understanding of atomic interactions, protein folding, and how enzymes mediate a reaction.

Nevertheless I suspect that within my lifetime, we will be able to input a chemical reaction into an AI model such as C02 + 2h20 > 202 + CH4 and get an enzyme that mediates that reaction to be energetically cheaper. Once that happens all kinds of things will become much more viable; carbon capture, plastic recycling, new medicines, mass production of graphene, the terraforming of other planets.

That being said, it would also have immense potential for the creation of new chemical and biological weapons.
We're all living in interesting times. Let us hope we survive them.
